news.Title: Monolithic Power Systems (MPWR) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript
news.Content:
Image source: The Motley Fool.

DATE

Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026

CALL PARTICIPANTS

Chief Executive Officer and Founder - Michael R. Hsing

Vice President and Chief Financial Officer - Tony Balow

Speaker - Arthur Lee

Full Conference Call Transcript

Operator: Good day, and thank you for standing by. Welcome to the Monolithic Power Systems Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. I would now like to hand the conference over to your speaker today, Arthur Lee. Please go ahead.

Arthur Lee: Earlier today, MPS released a written commentary on the results of its operations for the third quarter ended September 30, 2026. This document can be found on our website. Before we begin, I would like to remind everyone that in the course of today's presentation, we may make forward-looking statements and projections within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995 that involve risks and uncertainties. The risks, uncertainties and other factors that could cause actual results to differ from these forward-looking statements are identified in the safe harbor statements contained in the Q3 2026 earnings commentary and in our SEC filings, including our Form 10-K and Form 10-Q, which can be found on our website.

Our statements are made as of today, and we assume no obligation to update this information. Now I would like to turn the call over to Tony.

Tony Balow: Thanks, Arthur. Good afternoon, and for us, good morning from Shanghai, and welcome to our Q3 2026 earnings call. In Q3, MPS achieved another significant milestone, exceeding $1 billion in quarterly revenue for the first time. Q3 revenue of $1.2 billion was 22% higher than the second quarter of 2026 and 63% higher than the third quarter of 2025. During the quarter, our capacity surpassed $6 billion in annual revenue support. We expect to have $8 billion of capacity in place by the second half of 2027 on our way to $10 billion in support of our rapidly expanding business. In our enterprise data end market, we saw strong demand across existing customers, which we expect to continue into 2027.

In addition, using our in-house developed AI design tools, we significantly expanded our customer base in traditional areas as well as landing new wins in applications such as desktop AI designs. Beyond our strong enterprise data growth in automotive, we received first orders for our 48-volt power solutions and expect design wins for 48-volt and zonal architectures to be a driver of growth in 2027. We started ramping robotic solutions with sensor and motor control products across multiple geographies. We continue to increase our SAM with the ramp of our high-speed memory products. We landed our first large data converter design win, which we expect to ramp next year.

Story Continues

And we continue to build out our high-voltage portfolio and began sampling GaN-based solutions for use in 800-volt data center architectures, complementing our existing silicon carbide-based designs. And finally, in Q3, we repurchased over $450 million of our own stock. Overall, we see accelerated growth. Our diversified growth strategy is paying off. Operator, you may now open the webinar for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from Tore Svanberg with Stifel.

Tore Svanberg: Michael and Tony, congratulations on that $1 billion milestone. And to you, Tony, congratulations on your CFO appointment. I guess for my first question, you talked about accelerated growth. I was hoping you can maybe elaborate a little bit of that. I mean I'm sure you're not going to give us calendar '27 guidance, but you are on track to growing 50%, 60% this year. And especially in light of your $8 billion capacity and then $10 billion, when could we potentially see $10 billion capacity in place?

Michael R. Hsing: Yes. Thanks, Tore. See as Tony mentioned is only a few items, so we see beyond that. And I see this explosive growth period in the next few years. And even this year, you see the first 9 months, okay? And we don't see anything -- any signs of the slowdown.

Tony Balow: Yes. The other thing I'd add is I think as we've come into the second half, you started to see growth across multiple of our end markets, including like auto, which the ramp started here in Q3, and we've talked about continuing here through the second half. And then as we start to see applications like robotics begin to ramp, we'd expect that then to continue into the future. So I think it's not just the existing businesses, it's adding on the additional growth areas over time, which is really giving us confidence going forward.

Tore Svanberg: Very good. And as my follow-up, you mentioned the 800-volt GaN product sampling. Now that you are sampling GaN, could you maybe elaborate a little bit more, help us understand a little bit more the positioning there? Is this vertical GaN? Is it horizontal GaN? Is it your own process? Any more color you can help us there? And when do you expect to start to see some 800-volt GaN revenue?

Michael R. Hsing: Yes. We let -- it is based on MPS own development, which is later than we developed silicon carbide device. And we start to sampling that this type of solutions. We let our customers choose in either using GaN, the GaN is a new technology for everyone, okay? And for everyone adopting it in the data centers and the industrial automotive type of applications, okay? This is the first time. And we are always very cautious about the reliability. We want to achieve below 1 ppm failures and for these modules. And we let our customers choose, okay? GaN or silicon carbide. Silicon carbide is known, we know the data.

And so that's a very high reliability product and GaNs we have to ship somewhere 50 million units before we can say this is a good -- this is a new one for GaN, but we let our customers choose.

Tony Balow: Yes. I'll just add on it, I think all of the experience -- I was just going to add a few things there. This is just the experience we've already gained in data center, I think, puts us in a really good position to do what Michael is talking about in terms of making sure we can meet all the standards that customer requires. You asked a question on the timing of it. I think right now, we're still -- we've always kind of been late in '27 for I think kind of the 800-volt kind of architecture ramps with probably more in '28. I don't think our thinking on that has changed.

We're just obviously getting ahead of that design work now.

Michael R. Hsing: Even for our customers, they use both. They don't want to have a failure either. They use both solutions.

Operator: Our next question comes from Rick Schafer with Oppenheimer & Co.

Richard Schafer: Congratulations to you guys and congratulations, Tony, on the appointment. If I could ask a question on storage and compute for my first one, I was hoping maybe you could level set us on some of the moving parts in there. I mean, how does that segment split now if you look at SSD, HDD, DDR5, PMIC versus the PC, the VCore power piece? Because I know we all see PC units tracking down about 20% here in the second half. So I'm just curious, is that kind of what you guys are seeing on the PC side of that segment? And then how much is the storage piece growing? And what's it contributing?

Tony Balow: Yes, Rick, let me start, and then I'll let Michael come in. I think just kind of mechanically, if you look at it, the big driver of growth in that segment has been the DDR5, primarily on the PMIC solution. As we said, we're just starting the high-speed journey on the DDR5. We have seen pretty healthy growth over the past year or so on the hard disk drive and SSD part of that storage business as well. But clearly, DDR5 is the biggest portion of that. On notebook, sort of tactically, yes, I think we're -- we've been talking about this, and that's what we're seeing as well, right?

We're seeing not the same strength on notebook due to what's happening downstream with some of the memory constraints. But I think, if you look forward, I think we're still pretty bullish on notebook in the long term because we have really good technology and good share -- and then I think there's applications around AI that will continue to build out over time at the edge, of which notebook will play a part. So I think what you're seeing in the short term around notebook tracks with what you're seeing, Rick. But I think long term, I think we're still pretty high on what notebook could be for the company.

Michael R. Hsing: Yes. For that segment, we have a new products like a clock drivers and RCD. These all lined up and other than in addition to our power management product. These will be lined up for revenue in 2027 or '28. And we see even '28, these products will really ramping up, okay? So that's part of a TAM is much bigger than power management. And the notebooks, as Tony mentioned it, we will see this as a very fast growing market segments because after the manufacturing capacity opens up, that the segment will grow along with the desktop.

Tony Balow: If you sum that up a little bit, what we said for kind of the segment overall is with the puts and takes, it could be kind of flattish, up a couple of points year-over-year is kind of how we positioned it, but it's really a tale of 2 cities, as we've talked about with really strong storage and then the TAM just being limited on the notebook side.

Richard Schafer: Got it. And then if I could -- this is your first call with the CFO moniker. And I'm curious how you look at OpEx growth going forward? I mean, any meaningful changes to the prior targets that you guys have laid out? I mean, at these type of top line growth rates that Tore called out, 50%, 60% type top line, how fast can you actually scale R&D, et cetera? It seems like we're -- it seems like you guys are set for some pretty material operating leverage to be flowing through the model. Is that the right way to be thinking about it? Any rules of thumb in there?

Michael R. Hsing: Let me answer that part of the question, Rick. I never believe the big dollars R&D equivalent to a bigger result. It's -- for our business, it's inversely proportional to that. We just need some good ideas, good people that we're going to make everything happen.

Tony Balow: So yes, I think, Rick, you're not going to see us necessarily change our model. What we've seen pragmatically, though, as we start to get to higher levels of growth that we start to fall below our model range in terms of we just can't spend money that fast. But I completely can agree with Michael on that. It's about the efficiency of the R&D and the people that you get versus just spending more. But in general, I'd say at the growth rates that we've seen, for example, this year, you're going to fall below the model from an OpEx perspective.

Operator: Our next question comes from Quinn Bolton with Needham & Company.

Quinn Bolton: I'll echo my congratulations and Tony, congratulations on the new role. I guess I want to start with the enterprise data. Last quarter, you gave us a floor of 130%. With September results and December guidance, it kind of looks like you're tracking to maybe 150% growth. But wondering, Tony, if you might be able to level set us what a new floor growth for enterprise data might be? And then I know it's early, but any sort of thoughts on that segment as you look into 2027, what kind of growth rate you might be looking at in the forward case? And then I've got a follow-on in the comms business.

Tony Balow: Sure. Let me start just kind of with the -- to answer your question, straight. I think at this point, given what we've seen in Q3 and Q4, we're comfortable raising the floor from -- we were at 130% year-over-year. But to your point, I think we're comfortable with a floor of 150% year-over-year now going forward. On 2027, I think it's a little early for us to go put a percentage out at this time, but I'll start and Michael, I'm sure, will follow up in that. Structurally, the growth drivers that we're seeing this year are all intact, right, whether you see the diversification of customers, the growth in modules, the content gains as new platforms roll out.

And I think over time, as you start to see even stronger growth in GPU potentially driven by the Agentic AI workloads, that's going to be even a further tailwind out in time. So while a little early to call next year, I feel really good about the growth drivers.

Michael R. Hsing: Well, I see in the next years and beyond next years, and I'm very excited to see that we build our own data centers. And as Tony mentioned earlier, the result is a tremendous improvement. And so this is not in the data centers, but in MPS own servers. And all these server, we believe -- I believe it will change and change to a GaN type of servers, and again the hardware will change and that will trickle down to desktops and even the notebook I said earlier. And this type of growth, it will trickle down in the next year and the year after. We see those trends, these design activities is really happening.

And so this is not only this year, not only in the data centers, it will trickle down to all other areas.

Tony Balow: Do you have a follow-up on comms?

Quinn Bolton: Yes. It's obviously congrats on the nice growth. I think it was 43% sequentially. It really looks like it was a breakout quarter in September. Wondering if that was primarily driven by optical modules? Or are you seeing a broader set of contributors to that growth? And just any thoughts into the December quarter? Does that sort of pace of growth continue into December?

Tony Balow: It's a great question. And to take us back here, obviously, coming into the year, we obviously had very strong growth in optical modules. And what we added beginning of the year is what we've been calling the switch business. And I know I've talked about this before. But to answer your question, why are you starting to see the accelerated growth in that particular end market is because you are adding both of those growth drivers together, and we saw the effect really in Q3. And I think for the year, we've been positioning it is it's -- I think comms is going to be our second fastest-growing end market for sure.

It won't be quite as fast as enterprise data, but certainly won't be far behind. And just like enterprise data, I think if you go into next year, all of those growth drivers are intact. On optical modules, you see the transition to 1.6. That's not just a volume play, but there's a content play there as well. And then certainly, as we continue to build out additional sockets in the switch business, that's going to be a driver of growth as well. So I think right now, we really like the comms business, not just this year, but going into next year.

Michael R. Hsing: And on the macro economy and market segment predictions, I only care what is the design activity and what our customers are excited about it, what we're excited about it, all these new technology, new product introductions. And as I said earlier to [ market ], all these segments, we introduced the new product and all the design activities that give us an indication clearly the growth for even beyond next year.

Operator: Our next question comes from Joshua Buchalter with TD Cowen.

Joshua Buchalter: Congrats on the results and echoing the congrats to Tony on the CFO gig. Best of luck. I'll stick with policy and ask one on enterprise data and then one on another segment. Maybe can you comment on the diversity of enterprise data? Like how has that business evolved over the last year or 2 and looking into 2027? I would just be curious to hear how much you see coming from GPUs versus ASICs or even any comments you can help us on how much is coming from modules versus discrete at this point and expectations into '27?

Michael R. Hsing: Yes. Modules versus the chip design, chip power supplies, and then ICs on the chip all of them, okay? I mean even for the server side, and okay, we see some -- many activities and going through using modules because of the high current high-power demand. That's my comment, okay? And it's all segments -- from growth -- the real growth percentage, I'll let Tony to...

Tony Balow: Yes, I think -- and that -- I think it's an important point around this customer diversity that starting in the middle of 2025 until now, what we've seen is a really rapid growth in a lot of ASIC customers, which again are primarily using modules over time. And so that's benefited from a revenue diversity perspective as those carry the higher ASP associated with that. I think furthermore, what Michael was talking about in terms of how we've been using AI to create scale to allow us to go address even a longer tail of small customers over time, which may be big customers in the future.

And that's really what we try to do, go in every socket, not knowing who ultimately in the long term might grow into a sizable customer.

Michael R. Hsing: Yes. All we clearly see is that we have the huge beneficial from these artificial environment, these artificial intelligence based on these large language model. Of course, MPS [indiscernible] is internal. And it benefit us, it will benefit for everybody. And that's where I'm very optimistic about this and our growth trend will continue.

Joshua Buchalter: Maybe in the same theme of starting with small sockets that become big opportunities. Any context you can provide on how much revenue contribution we can expect from the initial high-speed data converter design win? And how big is that TAM as we think about you growing into this new market?

Michael R. Hsing: Yes. This is -- we can't tell because we have -- we just counted, these are over -- conservatively well over 6,000 products, okay? And we continue to develop newer products. So what we do is we do every segment in our best, far better than -- or to meet the new market demand. And we are much faster than any of our competitors. And as long as we do, the segments do the best and the revenue will come. And we don't -- we just don't know what -- which segment. 7, probably 8 years ago, we look at our product lines, look at the optical market segment, one of the perfect example.

We didn't know today was that high demand. And we got it in there. We serve our customers regardless of the large or small. And that's what happened today. I cannot predict next 10 years, next 5 years, we will be bigger, and we serve our small customers well.

Tony Balow: Yes. I think -- and again, to Michael's point, we're not ready to call the long term. We're just beginning that process. So I wouldn't necessarily say it moves the needle here in 2026. And I think as we get into next year, we'll talk more and see how that ramp goes.

Operator: Our next question comes from Will Stein with Truist Securities.

William Stein: First, on data center vertical power. I think there's still one meaningful customer doing lateral and I'm wondering if you can comment as to whether you think that converts to vertical in the coming year and whether that would necessarily require a module from you instead of some other sort of solution.

Michael R. Hsing: Certainly, okay, I don't want to speak for our customers, in particular that one customer. But I said earlier, and you know that what we did in the -- we predicted in the 2016 -- and for the server market, MPS solution is so small, and we have to use the adapter to meet the common footprint. And so when -- for the server market segment, we predicted and if you go above 600, 700 watts and you run out of peripheral and you have to use a smaller footprint. But the server GPU never get that never get to the 600, 700 watts, but the GPU did it, okay?

And as GPU power increase, I don't have a generalized numbers, okay? It will -- the power goes up, you run out of peripheral, you have to do vertical. And we said this many years earlier, okay? I still believe that very logical to me.

Tony Balow: Yes. I mean I'm just going to echo Michael. I think that we won't speak for that. Most of the industry has already moved to modules, right? And that's what we've seen in terms of content gains as well as the volume gains as we've gone through enterprise data. And I think that will be a great question for our customers. Yes, take a last jump [indiscernible].

William Stein: Great. And a different topic. Someone asked about the OpEx leverage. And I guess I understand that for the time being, with the rapid growth, you're going to sort of undershoot on spending, overshoot on margins. What about gross margin? I think the company has talked for a long time about 10 to 20 bps per quarter gross margin expansion. There was a time when you weren't in that range, and it seems like you are today. Any likelihood that because of the growth, you could exceed that expansion rate? Or should we still think about 10 bps to 20 bps is likely? Or any update there would be helpful.

Tony Balow: No. And thanks for calling out. Yes, you saw that we obviously did increase 10 basis points here in Q3. The midpoint of our guide in Q4 is kind of another 10 basis points. So I think we're kind of squarely in the model that we like, right? 55% to 60% is the sweet spot for sure. And within that being kind of slow, methodical about expansion. I think we're going to continue on that path. Structurally, I feel pretty good about that. We'll see what happens in the future.

But remember, what we don't want to do ever is put a bunch of gross margin in one quarter and then take it away the next quarter and move it around a bunch...

Michael R. Hsing: During the capacity constraint, we don't gouge our customers. And so we want to deliver to you guys a very consistent story. And I don't want to answer a question when the margins drops? And I want our MPS to keep it same business, same performance year-over-year -- quarter-over-quarter, year-over-year.

Tony Balow: That's right. So I think the model still holds. I'm very comfortable with that. And I think you called it out, but I'll highlight it again. I think if you look at the flow-through to operating margin, we've been growing operating margin, it's kind of a point a quarter almost. So we've seen a lot of expansion on the operating margin line.

Michael R. Hsing: We are in a making money business. And that's all I would point here.

Operator: Next question comes from Chris Caso with Wolfe Research.

Christopher Caso: Just following from the prior discussion, maybe you could talk about how you're dealing with rising costs. And obviously, costs are going up a lot of different places. There's a lot of talk of foundry wafer prices going higher. So to what extent are you passing that along? And as you go forward, does any of that result in pricing or any kind of revenue tailwind as you have to absorb some of those costs and pass them along to customers?

Michael R. Hsing: We definitely absorb some of the cost increase. And not that we don't increase the price, okay? And we some -- we share the cost with -- the cost increase with our customers.

Tony Balow: Yes, I think that's right, Chris. And I think if what you're asking is from some of the results, how much of that is from pricing, it's really not a significant contributor to the revenue growth that we've had. We are more just making sure that we don't dilute ourselves on the gross margin line.

Michael R. Hsing: Yes. Our customers have a very long memory.

Christopher Caso: Right. Okay. As a follow-up, it's a question on the 800-volt transition. And I know there's a lot of noise out there with regard to the pace of that transition. What -- in terms of MPS, how important is that to you in '27? And I guess maybe the question is, is it really 800 volts a very material driver of content in the EV segment? Or is the majority of that still going to wind up in the existing low power -- I'm sorry, low-voltage designs?

Michael R. Hsing: Yes, we don't want to add more voices, okay? We don't talk about it until the revenue for sure will come, okay? I do see the revenue for sure will come. Not this quarter, not next quarter, probably end of the '27 and 2028. And it's clearly the DC supply for high power demand and will be the trend, will be the data center, all will convert it to that. And the power savings is, I think, beyond like single digit -- single-digit percentage improvement versus the traditional power supply. I see this is even beyond the data center. And if the data center can improve, let's say, 5%, where do you get the 5% money returns?

And all the commercial building, even residential, they all can be like this, 400 volt these are in -- there will be -- in Europe will be 800 volts in U.S. will be 400 volts. And that these will be a significant power savings across the board. That's what I'm excited about this opportunity now.

Tony Balow: Yes. I mean I'll even try to just address the question the other way, which is when we talked about our -- how we are excited about growth in enterprise data, it's not because we're -- we have a big built-in ramp on 800 volt. It's really around the existing customers, the new customers, transition to modules, all the things that we've been talking about, Chris. So if you're kind of trying to figure out how much of that excitement was just at 800 volt, I really think the business we have today is what we're confident in.

Michael R. Hsing: Yes. MPS now we're using our own building do a lot experiment, using these 800 volts and using the technology and see what the power saving is.

Operator: Our next question comes from Sebastien Naji with William Blair.

Sebastien Cyrus Naji: Congratulations, Tony, on your appointment. I wanted to maybe just ask my first question, given some of the news around integrated voltage regulators and the acquisition of Empower by Analog Devices, maybe could you just give us your view on this technology and whether you see it as a competitive risk in the AI data center or the larger data center?

Michael R. Hsing: Yes, we don't comment on other companies' activities. And we have our own solutions. We have our own and we can deliver whatever customer wanted. And this is not BS talks, we do have multiple beyond what you guys beyond the noise levels. And we have those technologies and we can deliver. And the GPU evolves very quickly, the power levels, the architecture and in terms of the power delivery. And we don't talk about those until we have -- we see -- clearly see where the revenue will come.

Sebastien Cyrus Naji: Okay. Okay. Great. That's helpful. We'll look forward to those announcements when those products are ready. Maybe moving to something that's a little bit closer to your heart, Michael, which is the building automation opportunity. I think last quarter, you talked about $40 billion to $50 billion in size, but that the real bottleneck was the software still needed to catch up. Can you maybe just talk a little bit about the progress that's been made here as we get to the end of the year?

Michael R. Hsing: Well, good questions, okay? That's my baby project. And we just have installed in our 1 million square feet building. That's in China. And we -- as I said just a minute ago, we're experimenting our own AC to DC power. These are for 800-volt supply. And for across the building, -- and that project -- these projects just started. But in terms of turning to a $50 billion revenue will take some time. We don't know how to get there yet, but the goal is very clear. And we will get there. There's a lot of software involved in it, okay? But on the hardware side, we pretty much have every single component.

And our single -- our components, our chips, our module technology is far better than -- sorry to say these are the current existing technology. These are 50-year old, and we will do some significant improvement on it.

Operator: Our next question comes from Kelsey Chia with Citi.

Wei Chia: Congrats on the great results again. And Tony, congrats on your well-deserved appointment. So my question is on the switching business. So to what extent is that contributing to the strong communications growth that we saw in third quarter? And how should we think about the ramp as we head into 2027 and if that business is accretive to gross margins?

Tony Balow: Yes, I'll start on that one. So we're obviously not going to start guiding sub end markets a little bit. But certainly, from just a percentage basis, it's been growing very quickly, probably on a percentage basis, the fastest-growing sub end market inside of communications just because it started from a very low amount at the beginning of the year. As we go forward, again, I still think that and optical modules are going to be significant growth drivers for communications into 2027. On the margin side, I think if you look at all of our end markets, plus or minus, they'll all operate around the corporate average because to Michael's point, we have north of 6,000, 7,000 products.

And so if you look at the distribution of that, basically, what we said is as we grow this, we don't think growing one end market over another will necessarily take us out of our model. And so right now, I would still take MPS as a total kind of in that 55% to 60% range with sort of the slow methodical expansion when we can provide it versus worrying about whether growth in one end market would take you out of model.

Wei Chia: And my second question is on the industrial end market. I mean, very strong growth this quarter as well. What drove that strong growth this quarter? And if you could talk about the ramp of the robotic solutions? And how do you see that ramping in '27?

Michael R. Hsing: The robotics, we -- I tried to enter the robotics in 2016. On the Analyst Day, we talked about robotics, that's the area we're focused on. We have a product for these sensors and motor controls -- and I didn't know what I was talking about, the revenue didn't come, okay? And now it shows up. And I think this is still at the very beginning, once the vision for the recognition and visual recognition and improved from using the AI-based vision improvement technology. These robots, as you know, they will propagate in everyday life. So I see this -- that's the future. And the revenue would be significantly higher than that.

Tony Balow: Yes. I think the only thing I'd add kind of on the overall segment is, I think this year, we still look at it as just piling up design wins in robotics and other places and really look for more of that in 2027. The growth in the quarter was fairly broad-based, but I think you start to see a lot of these other design wins come to turn into revenue in the future. So I think that in kind of consumer and industrial, 2026, I think, really does still remain mostly about winning all the designs that support future growth.

Operator: Our next question comes from Joe Quatrochi with Wells Fargo.

Joseph Quatrochi: My congrats as well, Tony. Maybe just kind of a finer point on the expansion of capacity to $8 billion. I can appreciate that you can't grow OpEx as fast and you don't need to grow as fast. But how do we think about like maybe some of the investments you have to make on the working capital side or go-to-market side to support that?

Tony Balow: Yes. I think on -- one of the nice things about being in a fabless model, right, is we don't have to dig a hole and pour concrete into it.

Michael R. Hsing: We don't make it and it will wake our brain generally.

Tony Balow: That's right. So we -- I don't anticipate at this point seeing a large increase in capital intensity just to go ramp this capacity, right? So it gives us a lot of flexibility. As a matter of fact, I am personally just amazed at the amount of capacity we've been able to put on just even over the last year. And I think the operations team has done a tremendous job. But I don't see it necessarily reflecting the overall OpEx at this point or any kind of change to our capital structure just to put on that extra capacity.

Joseph Quatrochi: Okay. And then maybe as a follow-up, I think auto is continuing to see some inflection. Can you just talk about the breadth of demand you're seeing there from a geographic perspective and how we think about like the design pipeline looking into '27?

Michael R. Hsing: It's of course, geographic in U.S. side, Europe side and also in Asia, China. We see -- in China, particularly, we see a lot of activities. And so that's probably the world. And we -- as we said -- as I said earlier, we can't predict which market segment. And that's our diversified growth strategy. And some years, one segment is good, even with a mature market and some years, one market segment is good and the other one is not so good, okay? And in the last few years, all of a sudden, the GPU market happened or the optical market and the revenue happened. And so we didn't anticipate it. We just provide the best highest performance product.

Our customers will realize it.

Tony Balow: Yes. The only thing I'd add is I think the reason we've been pretty confident on the ramp in the second half is because it is so diverse amongst customers and regions and not dependent just on one. You've seen that same level of customer diversity grow in auto over the past several years, like we've been talking about in enterprise data. And the pipeline is similar, right? It's very geographically diverse and very customer diverse. We were just very excited to start seeing some of the architectural transitions that we've been talking about in sort of 48-volt and zonal because those sort of form the next wave of growth for us.

Michael R. Hsing: We're not predicting what the market is.

Operator: Our last question comes from Gary Mobley with StoneX.

Gary Mobley: Congrats Tony, again. I wanted to ask about what you might be signaling in your capacity milestones. You're currently at $6 billion in production capacity, which I assume supports your 2027 outlook. It doesn't take much to get there, just extrapolating out Q4 revenue guidance. And you're expected to be at $8 billion in capacity exiting fiscal year '27. So should we think about that in terms of the revenue velocity exiting fiscal year '27?

Michael R. Hsing: It doesn't take much to get there, oh, come on, this is the market that move the numbers. There's a lot of work behind it.

Tony Balow: Yes. I'll add, so right now, I think what we're trying to strongly signal is that just like we've been doing in the past 20 years, we're making sure that capacity stays ahead of the business. And in a world where there's a lot of narrative around there being tightness, we wanted to be very clear to you and our customers how we're growing capacity to support that business. So I think, again, it's too early to go right into a quarterly revenue ramp and what that means for 2027.

But we wanted to make sure it was loud and clear was that we see the demand coming, and we're going to make sure capacity is there to deal with it.

Gary Mobley: And on inventory, I just want to confirm that the distribution inventory is still within that normal 5- to 8-week range. And then it looks like your internal inventory is down to 117 days based on a forward revenue guide basis, and that's been trickling down. Are you inventoried properly to support sales, I guess, is really the question.

Tony Balow: I think right now, we're still on the channel side, certainly in the lean end of our range like we've been for some time now. And internally, I think we grew dollars on a gross basis, right? But obviously, as the revenues ramp, that's come down from a days perspective. So I think that our range certainly hasn't changed, and it's something that as we increase our capacity and our wafer starts, we'll make sure that we're positioned for the business. But right now, it's not limiting us on the business.

Operator: This concludes the question-and-answer session. I would now like to turn it back to Tony Balow for closing remarks.

Tony Balow: All right. Thank you, operator, and thank you all for joining us for this conference call today. I look forward to speaking with you on the next call for the fourth quarter and full year '26 revenue guidance. Thank you again, and have a great day.

Operator: This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.

news.Title: AXTI Q3 Earnings Beat on Record InP Sales and Margin Gains
news.Content:
AXT, Inc. AXTI reported non-GAAP earnings of 41 cents per share in the third quarter of 2026, surpassing the Zacks Consensus Estimate of 31 cents by 32.26%. The company had recorded a non-GAAP loss of 3 cents per share in the year-ago quarter.

Revenues rose 162% year over year and 54% sequentially to $73.4 million, topping the consensus estimate by 11.05%. Strong indium phosphide (InP) sales to AI data-center customers and higher manufacturing productivity supported the beat. Backlog surpassed $500 million.

AXTI's InP Revenues Hit a New High in Q3

InP revenues reached $54.3 million, the highest level in AXT's history. Data-center demand accounted for the bulk of InP sales as customers deployed high-speed optical components.

The shift to 800G and 1.6T transceiver modules is fueling demand for InP-based lasers and photodetectors that move data across dense AI computing systems. Management also expects growing demand for continuous-wave lasers used in next-generation optical interconnects.

AXT Inc Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise

AXT Inc price-consensus-eps-surprise-chart | AXT Inc Quote

AXT's GaAs Sales Rise, Raw Materials Remain Key

Gallium arsenide (GaAs) revenues totaled $9.1 million in the third quarter. Demand for semi-insulating and semiconducting wafers increased sequentially, supported by wireless devices, industrial robotics and data-center laser applications.

Germanium substrate revenues reached $344,000, while consolidated raw-material businesses contributed $9.7 million. The company's five largest customers represented about 35% of total revenues, with one customer accounting for more than 10%. Management expects some GaAs markets to soften seasonally in the fourth quarter.

AXTI's Margins Widen on Volume, Mix and Pricing

Non-GAAP gross margin rose to 56.1% from 45% in the prior quarter and 22.4% a year earlier. Increased volumes, a richer InP product mix, improved factory efficiency and higher selling prices for InP wafers contributed to the expansion.

Non-GAAP operating expenses increased to $11.7 million from $10.2 million sequentially and $6.7 million a year earlier. Even with higher spending, non-GAAP operating income jumped to $29.5 million from $11.2 million in the previous quarter, against a $0.4 million operating loss a year ago.

AXT Pushes Ahead With Capacity Expansion

AXT exceeded its initial 2026 target to double InP capacity by August. Management now anticipates exiting 2026 with about 2.75 to three times its year-end 2025 capacity, followed by another doubling in 2027. The company is also planning to convert an adjacent building into manufacturing space.

New proprietary crystal-growth furnaces are helping increase wafer output. Six-inch InP lines are entering pilot production, while customers are transitioning from three-inch to higher-value four-inch wafers. AXT expects the shift in laser substrates to accelerate in 2027, creating further pricing and margin opportunities.

Story Continues

AXTI's Backlog Surges Amid Tight Wafer Supply

Management said demand still exceeds InP supply, with all customers on allocation. The order book spans multiyear agreements, shorter contracts and spot purchase orders extending into 2027. Orders from Chinese customers have also increased, with domestic shipments avoiding export-permit requirements.

During the quarter, AXT signed a supply agreement with Lumentum and received a $43.5 million wafer prepayment. The advance remains a liability until related wafers ship. Management said many orders carry lead times exceeding nine months and it is limiting new long-term commitments to preserve pricing flexibility.

AXT Strengthens Liquidity and Funding Options

Cash, cash equivalents and investments were $825.9 million as of Sept. 30, 2026, up from $748.8 million at June 30. Days sales outstanding improved to 49 following customer prepayments, while net inventory increased approximately $7.4 million sequentially.

The majority-owned Tongmei subsidiary agreed to a private equity financing of up to $545 million to fund wafer and raw-material capacity expansion in China. If fully subscribed, AXT would retain approximately 73.4% ownership. Tongmei is also pursuing a Hong Kong stock market listing.

AXTI Sees Higher Q4 Earnings and Margins

AXT has approximately $90 million in revenues for the fourth quarter of 2026, supported by existing export permits or shipments requiring no permit. AXT expressed high confidence in realizing that amount, while InP is expected to account for most of the sequential sales increase.

Non-GAAP earnings are projected at 57-59 cents per share, with GAAP earnings expected at 56-58 cents. Non-GAAP operating expenses are pegged at roughly $13 million versus $14 million on a GAAP basis. The share-count assumption is 66.1 million. Gross margin could exceed 60%.

AXTI's Zacks Rank & Stocks to Consider

AXT currently carries a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold).

Camtek CAMT, Fastly FSLY and Microchip MCHP are among the better-ranked stocks that investors can consider in the broader Zacks Computer and Technology sector. Currently, Camtek sports a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy), while Enovix Corporation and Microchip carry a Zacks Rank #2 (Buy) each. You can see the complete list of today's Zacks #1 Rank stocks here .

Camtek's shares have returned 19.1% year to date. CAMT is scheduled to report its third-quarter 2026 results on Nov. 4.

Fastly's shares have surged 151.8% year to date. FSLY is slated to report its third-quarter 2026 results on Nov. 4.

Microchip's shares have gained 27.4% year to date. MCHP is scheduled to report its fiscal second-quarter 2027 results on Nov. 5, 2026.

news.Title: AMD Expands AI Footprint With Meta: Can It Outpace NVDA & AVGO?
news.Content:
Advanced Micro Devices AMD is benefiting from accelerating demand for artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure, expanding hyperscaler partnerships and growing adoption of its EPYC processors and Instinct GPUs. The company recently strengthened its strategic partnership with Meta Platforms to support the latter's superintelligence infrastructure, enhancing its competitive position against NVIDIA NVDA and Broadcom AVGO. The collaboration spans CPUs, GPUs, networking, rack-scale systems and software, positioning AMD to capture a larger share of hyperscaler AI investments.

AMD's Helios rack-scale solutions are undergoing testing at Meta ahead of broader deployment, while EPYC processors power Meta's Muse AI agent. Meta has deployed millions of EPYC CPUs and plans to adopt sixth-generation EPYC processors. AMD Instinct GPUs support Meta's AI training, ranking and recommendation workloads, with plans to deploy customized Instinct GPUs based on the MI450 architecture. The collaboration encompasses ROCm software optimization, future MI500 GPUs and gigawatt-scale AI infrastructure. AMD also plans to invest $1 billion in Meta's equity offering.

AMD's expanding AI ecosystem strengthens its growth prospects. Partnerships with OpenAI, Anthropic and Microsoft support broader adoption of its Helios platform. In the second quarter of 2026, Data Center revenues surged 107% year over year to $6.7 billion, driven by robust EPYC and Instinct demand. AMD expects the Data Center business to more than double in 2027, while server CPU revenues are projected to increase more than 80% year over year in the second half of 2026 and more than 70% in 2027.

AMD's expanding AI infrastructure portfolio, stronger hyperscaler partnerships and robust demand for EPYC processors and Instinct accelerators position it well to challenge NVIDIA and Broadcom and drive top-line growth. For the third quarter of 2026, AMD expects revenues of approximately $13 billion, plus or minus $300 million. The midpoint implies growth of roughly 41% year over year and 13% sequentially.

How Competitors Fare Against AMD

AMD's prospects suffer from stiff competition from companies like NVIDIA and Broadcom, which are major competitors in the AI space.

NVIDIA's accelerated computing platform remains central to AI training, inference and agentic workloads as customers scale model deployment. In the second quarter of fiscal 2027, revenues rose 106% year over year to $96.2 billion, while Compute & Networking revenues increased 114% to $88.3 billion. Data Center revenues reached $89 billion, up 117%, with Blackwell Ultra driving the expansion.

Broadcom is benefiting from expanding AI infrastructure spending, with custom XPUs and networking driving semiconductor growth while VMware supports infrastructure software. Multiyear engagements with six XPU customers, broader Ethernet adoption and rising AI deployments provide long-term revenue visibility. Broadcom now expects fiscal 2026 AI semiconductor revenues of $58 billion, up 186% year over year and above its prior $56 billion outlook.

news.Title: MPWR Q3 Earnings Surpass Estimates on Enterprise Data Strength
news.Content:
Monolithic Power Systems, Inc. MPWR reported third-quarter 2026 non-GAAP earnings of $8.19 per share, which increased 73.2% year over year and beat the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $7.80 by 5%. Revenues surged 63.1% to $1.20 billion, beating the consensus mark of $1.16 billion by 3.6%.

Record sales reflected strong demand for artificial intelligence (AI) and server power solutions, supported by expanding customer relationships and higher module content. Enterprise Data revenues jumped 164.6% year over year, accounting for 42.1% of total sales.

MPWR's Profitability Expands Despite Higher Costs

GAAP net income increased 50.8% to $271.1 million, or $5.51 per share, from $179.8 million, or $3.74 per share, a year earlier. Non-GAAP net income climbed 77.3% to $402.7 million. GAAP operating income rose to $357.7 million from $195.2 million.

Non-GAAP gross margin expanded 20 basis points (bps) year over year to 55.7%. Non-GAAP operating expenses increased 38.4% to $205.3 million, while the non-GAAP operating margin improved 320 bps to 38.6%.

Stock-based compensation and related expenses totaled $106.3 million compared with $53.5 million in the preceding quarter. Management reiterated its preference for gradual gross margin expansion while maintaining pricing discipline amid rising supplier costs.

Monolithic Power Systems, Inc. Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise

Monolithic Power Systems, Inc. price-consensus-eps-surprise-chart | Monolithic Power Systems, Inc. Quote

Monolithic's Enterprise Data Business Accelerates

Enterprise Data revenues reached $506.7 million, up 33.2% sequentially. Higher sales of power management solutions for AI and server applications drove growth, supported by stronger demand across existing customers.

Management raised its 2026 Enterprise Data revenue growth floor to 150% from 130%. Increasing adoption of power modules, customer diversification and higher content per computing platform remain major drivers. Application-specific integrated circuit customers have also contributed to demand for higher-value modules.

Storage and Computing revenues increased 3% year over year to $192.2 million but declined 3.8% sequentially. DDR5 power management products and storage applications supported sales, while weaker notebook demand, partly related to downstream memory constraints, remained a headwind.

MPWR's Communications and Automotive Sales Rise

Communications revenues surged 134.7% year over year to $187.4 million, representing 15.6% of total sales. Sequential growth of 42.5% reflected higher demand for power solutions used in optical modules and network switches.

Management expects optical module upgrades, including the transition to 1.6-terabit technology, and additional switching applications to support growth into 2027. Communications is expected to remain the company's second-fastest-growing end market.

Automotive revenues advanced 19.2% to $180.7 million, primarily benefiting from higher sales of advanced driver-assistance system power solutions. Monolithic received initial orders for its 48-volt power products, with 48-volt and zonal electrical architectures expected to drive further design opportunities in 2027.

Story Continues

Monolithic Broadens Its Industrial Product Portfolio

Industrial revenues increased 29% year over year to $71.4 million, reflecting higher sales of power sources. The company began ramping robotics solutions featuring sensors and motor control products across multiple geographic markets.

Consumer revenues declined 11.6% year over year to $64 million, although sales improved 12.6% sequentially. Management continues to prioritize new design wins across industrial and consumer applications to support future revenue opportunities.

The company also secured its first major data converter design win, with revenues ramp-up expected in 2027. Its expanding high-speed memory portfolio includes additional clock driver and registered clock driver products, which management expects to contribute in 2027 and 2028.

MPWR Expands Capacity and Maintains Liquidity

Cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments totaled $1.09 billion at September quarter-end, down from $1.41 billion in the preceding quarter. Operating cash flow increased to $289.9 million from $227.9 million.

Inventories increased to $764.9 million from $675.8 million, while inventory days based on current-quarter revenues declined to 130 from 140. The company repurchased $453.4 million of shares during the quarter.

Annual revenue-supporting capacity exceeded $6 billion, with management targeting $8 billion by the second half of 2027. The company also began sampling gallium nitride solutions for 800-volt data center architectures, complementing its silicon carbide offerings.

Monolithic Projects Higher Q4 Revenues

For the fourth quarter of 2026, management expects revenues between $1.315 billion and $1.385 billion. Non-GAAP gross margin is projected between 55.5% and 56.1%, while non-GAAP operating expenses are expected to be in the range of $216.8 million to $220.8 million.

GAAP operating expenses are forecast between $334 million and $342 million. Management expects a non-GAAP tax rate of 15% for 2026.

In October, the board authorized an additional $500 million in share repurchases, bringing the total current authorization to $1 billion after third-quarter buybacks.

news.Title: NVTS Gears Up to Report Q3 Earnings: Buy, Sell or Hold the Stock?
news.Content:
Navitas Semiconductor NVTS is scheduled to report its third-quarter 2026 results on Nov. 3, 2026.

Navitas Semiconductor anticipates revenues of $13.5 million (+/- $0.5 million) for the third quarter of 2026. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for second-quarter revenues is pegged at $13.48 million, suggesting a year-over-year increase of 33.3%.

The consensus mark for loss is pegged at 4 cents per share for the third quarter of 2026, unchanged over the past 30 days. NVTS reported a loss of 5 cents per share in the year-ago quarter.

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

Navitas Semiconductor's bottom-line results have matched the Zacks Consensus Estimate in three of the trailing four quarters, while beating once, with the average surprise being 5%.

Navitas Semiconductor Corporation Price and EPS Surprise

Navitas Semiconductor Corporation price-eps-surprise | Navitas Semiconductor Corporation Quote

Earnings Whispers for NVTS

Our proven model does not conclusively predict an earnings beat for Navitas Semiconductor this time. The combination of a positive Earnings ESP and a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy), 2 (Buy) or 3 (Hold) increases the odds of an earnings beat, which is not the case here.

Navitas Semiconductor has an Earnings ESP of 0.00% and carries a Zacks Rank #3 at present. You can uncover the best stocks to buy or sell before they are reported with our Earnings ESP Filter. You can see the complete list of today's Zacks #1 Rank stocks here.

Factors Likely to Influence NVTS' Q3 Results

Navitas Semiconductor is a well-known provider of power semiconductors, driven by its gallium nitride (GaN) business, under GaNFast, GaNSafe and GaNSense brands, along with silicon carbide (SiC) devices. Navitas Semiconductor is expected to have benefited from the growing demand for power that is served by the company's GaN and SiC technologies.

Navitas Semiconductor is shifting its focus toward high-power markets, such as artificial intelligence (AI) data centers, performance computing, energy and grid infrastructure, and industrial electrification. Its GaN and SiC chips are well-suited for new high-voltage systems that need more efficient power use. This strategic move aligns with the company's Navitas 2.0 strategy, under which the company is reallocating resources toward high-power markets, pruning lower-margin mobile business and working more closely with hyperscalers, graphics processing unit vendors and system OEMs.

Navitas Semiconductor's inclusion in NVIDIA's new 800-volt AI factory ecosystem is an important step. The new architecture shifts data center power distribution from traditional AC/DC stages to a high-voltage DC approach that requires faster, more efficient power electronics. This creates an opening for Navitas Semiconductor's GaN and high-voltage SiC technologies, both of which are now part of the NVIDIA-led ecosystem.

Story Continues

Navitas Semiconductor remains one of the few companies offering both GaN and SiC solutions across the power chain, from the grid to the data center rack. During the second quarter of 2026, management noted increasing adoption of GaN in high-end computing applications, including chargers above 200 watts and a recently launched 1,600-watt platform for high-performance gaming systems. As AI infrastructure spending continues to grow, Navitas Semiconductor remains well-positioned to benefit from higher demand for its GaN and SiC products. The above-mentioned factors are likely to have contributed to the company's prospects in the to-be-reported quarter.

However, NVTS' Navitas 2.0 strategy involves moving away from mobile charging and consumer electronics toward higher-power AI and industrial markets. While this may improve long-term growth, it also introduces meaningful near-term revenue volatility. The company is effectively walking away from markets where it already had product traction and revenue history in exchange for newer markets with longer design cycles and more demanding qualification requirements. This transition could create revenue volatility over the next several quarters.

NVTS Price Performance & Stock Valuation

Navitas Semiconductor shares have plunged 31.7% over the past year, underperforming the Zacks Electronics - Semiconductors industry's growth of 13.9%. Compared to other major players in the semiconductor space, NVTS has underperformed Lam Research LRCX, FormFactor FORM and Applied Materials AMAT. Over the past year, shares of Lam Research, FormFactor and Applied Materials have rallied 61.5%, 77.3% and 80.8%, respectively.

One-Year Price Return Performance

Navitas Semiconductor is currently trading at a higher price-to-sales (P/S) multiple compared with the industry. NVTS' forward 12-month P/S ratio sits at 36.67X, significantly higher than the industry's forward 12-month P/S ratio of 4.50X.

NVTS Forward 12-Month P/S Ratio

Navitas Semiconductor stock also trades at a higher P/S multiple compared with other industry peers, including Lam Research, FormFactor and Applied Materials. At present, Lam Research, FormFactor and Applied Materials have P/S multiples of 8.61X, 7.34X and 6.46X, respectively.

Investment Consideration for Navitas Semiconductor

Navitas Semiconductor is in a good position to benefit from the fast growth of AI data centers. Its GaN and SiC chips are well-suited for new high-voltage systems that need more efficient power use. Navitas Semiconductor's inclusion in NVIDIA's next-generation 800-volt DC "AI factory" positions NVTS in a large, fast-growing market where power design is becoming a priority, which bodes well for the company's prospects.

However, NVTS faces near-term challenges due to weakness in its China business, where the company has decided to prune its low-margin mobile business and low-end consumer business, which have not yet been fully offset by growth in high-power segments. These are likely to have hurt the company's prospects in the near term.

Conclusion: Hold Navitas Semiconductor Stock Right Now

Navitas Semiconductor is well-positioned to ride on the long-term growth in the AI data center market. The company's GaN and high-voltage SiC products now play a role in NVIDIA's new 800-volt power setup, which shows that the technology is relevant and in demand. If the company executes well, it could see better margins, a stronger product mix and a clearer path to stable long-term growth.

However, near-term risks from its decision to deprioritize its lower-margin mobile and consumer business, along with the company's high valuation, warrant a cautious approach to the stock.

news.Title: Twilio Q3 Earnings Beat Estimates on Strong Revenue Growth
news.Content:
Twilio Inc. TWLO reported better-than-expected third-quarter 2026 results, with both earnings and revenues surpassing the Zacks Consensus Estimate. Non-GAAP earnings of $1.65 per share beat the consensus mark by 13%. The bottom line increased 32% from the year-ago quarter's earnings of $1.25 per share, driven by robust revenue growth and operating leverage.

The cloud-based communications platform provider reported revenues of $1.56 billion, surpassing the consensus estimate by 3.1%. Revenues increased 20% year over year, driven by broad-based product strength and growing AI-related demand. The dollar-based net expansion rate was 114%, up from 109% a year ago.

TWLO's Q3 Revenue Growth Drivers

Twilio's organic revenues increased 16% year over year to $1.50 billion. Organic growth excludes incremental U.S. carrier pass-through fees and acquisition-related revenues. The company benefited from healthy demand across messaging, voice and software add-ons, alongside sustained momentum among AI-native customers.

Messaging revenues grew 24% year over year, supported by higher volumes and increased adoption of WhatsApp and Rich Communication Services. Incremental U.S. carrier fees contributed approximately seven percentage points to messaging revenue growth. Messaging accounted for 59% of total revenues during the quarter.

Twilio Inc. Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise

Twilio Inc. price-consensus-eps-surprise-chart | Twilio Inc. Quote

Voice revenues increased more than 20%, reflecting higher usage volumes and growing adoption of software add-ons. The self-serve channel registered revenue growth exceeding 30%, while independent software vendor revenues advanced more than 20%. Software add-on revenues grew more than 25%, and support and services revenues increased more than 30%.

Twilio's AI Momentum Supports Customer Expansion

Twilio witnessed continued adoption of its AI-enabled communications capabilities, including Conversation Relay, Conversational Intelligence and Branded Calling. Management highlighted growing demand from AI-native businesses deploying voice agents and expanding their usage across multiple communication channels.

The company secured several notable customer agreements during the quarter. Ushur signed a seven-figure expansion involving voice AI capabilities, while Gong renewed a seven-figure agreement. Twilio also secured its first eight-figure Conversations deal with a health insurance provider, underscoring growing enterprise interest in AI-powered customer engagement.

Story Continues

Management noted that voice AI represents approximately 1% of overall voice interactions, highlighting the early stage of adoption. Twilio is also developing identity verification capabilities for AI agents, with an offering currently in private beta and general availability planned for 2027.

TWLO's Profitability Improves Despite Carrier Fees

Non-GAAP gross profit increased 18% year over year to $767.8 million. However, non-GAAP gross margin contracted 90 basis points year over year to 49.2%, primarily due to $53 million of incremental U.S. carrier pass-through fees. Excluding these fees, gross margin would have expanded 80 basis points.

Non-GAAP income from operations surged 39% year over year to $325.7 million. Non-GAAP operating margin expanded 290 basis points to approximately 21%, reflecting strong gross profit growth and cost efficiencies. Operating income benefited from approximately $11 million in platform credits.

Twilio's Cash Generation Remains Strong

Net cash provided by operating activities reached $389.2 million compared with $263.6 million in the prior-year quarter. Free cash flow increased approximately 49% year over year to $369.6 million, with a free cash flow margin of 24%, up from 19%.

Twilio ended the third quarter with $1.06 billion in cash and cash equivalents and $1.83 billion in short-term marketable securities. Long-term debt stood at $993.6 million. The company repurchased $127.2 million of shares during the quarter, leaving approximately $700 million under its existing authorization.

TWLO Raises Its 2026 Outlook

For 2026, Twilio raised its reported revenue growth outlook to 20% from 18-18.5% and its organic revenue growth projection to 15% from 13-13.5%. The company also increased its non-GAAP income from operations and free cash flow guidance to $1.19-$1.20 billion each compared with the previous range of $1.135-$1.155 billion.

For the fourth quarter of 2026, Twilio expects revenues between $1.595 billion and $1.605 billion, indicating reported growth of 17-17.5% and organic growth of 11-12%. Non-GAAP income from operations is projected at $300-$310 million, with non-GAAP earnings of $1.48-$1.53 per share.

Twilio Provides an Upbeat 2027 Preliminary Outlook

Management expects organic revenue growth of at least 10% in 2027, exceeding its earlier long-term framework of 7-8%. Non-GAAP gross profit growth is anticipated to remain broadly aligned with organic revenue growth.

Twilio also projects non-GAAP income from operations and free cash flow of at least $1.35 billion each in 2027.

Twilio's Zacks Rank & Other Stocks to Consider

Currently, TWLO carries a Zacks Rank #2 (Buy).

Some other top-ranked stocks in the broader Zacks Computer and Technology sector are Analog Devices ADI, Autodesk ADSK and Cisco Systems CSCO, each carrying a Zacks Rank #2 at present. You can see the complete list of today's Zacks #1 Rank (Strong Buy) stocks here.

Shares of Analog Devices have rallied 85.3% year to date. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for ADI's fiscal 2026 earnings is pegged at $13.00 per share, up by 4 cents over the past 30 days, indicating an increase of 66.9% year over year.

Shares of Autodesk have plunged 19.6% year to date. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for ADSK's fiscal 2027 earnings is pegged at $12.62 per share, unchanged over the past 30 days, indicating a rise of 21% year over year.

Cisco Systems shares have surged 50.5% year to date. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for CSCO's fiscal 2027 earnings is pegged at $5.11 per share, unchanged over the past 30 days, indicating an increase of 18% year over year.

news.Title: ASE Technology Q3 Earnings Beat Estimates on AI-Driven LEAP Growth
news.Content:
ASE Technology Holding ASX reported third-quarter 2026 earnings of 37 cents per ADS, which increased 125.3% year over year and beat the Zacks Consensus Estimate by 8.8%.

Revenues surged 44.8% year over year and 27.8% sequentially to NT$244.16 billion. In U.S. dollar terms, revenues of $7.64 billion surpassed the Zacks Consensus Estimate by 3.3%. Results reflected robust artificial intelligence (AI)-driven demand for Leading-edge Advanced Packaging (LEAP) services, with Assembly, Testing and Materials (ATM) revenues climbing 51% year over year.

ASX ATM Growth Accelerates on LEAP Demand

ATM revenues totaled NT$151.49 billion, up 20.1% sequentially and 51% year over year. Packaging revenues surged 52.5% to NT$122.95 billion, while testing revenues advanced 42.8% to NT$26.30 billion.

Management cited strong demand across LEAP and conventional semiconductor services, with capacity operating at or near full utilization. Faster-than-expected installations of LEAP capacity supported revenue growth, while demand continued to exceed available supply across advanced and mainstream packaging operations.

ASE Technology Holding Co., Ltd. Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise

ASE Technology Holding Co., Ltd. price-consensus-eps-surprise-chart | ASE Technology Holding Co., Ltd. Quote

ASE Technology Revenue Mix Shifts Toward Computing

Computing represented 34% of ATM revenues, up from 25% in the year-ago quarter. Communication's contribution declined to 38% from 45%, while automotive, consumer and other applications accounted for 28%.

By service type, bumping, flip-chip, wafer-level packaging and system-in-package services contributed 51% of ATM revenues. Wire bonding accounted for 24%, testing represented 17%, other services contributed 6%, and materials made up 2%.

Management expects computing applications to remain a major growth driver through 2027 and 2028, supported by increasing LEAP adoption in high-performance computing and other advanced semiconductor applications.

ASE Technology's EMS Results Stay Mixed

Electronic Manufacturing Services (EMS) revenues increased 35.4% year over year and 42.1% sequentially to NT$93.47 billion. Consumer applications represented 41% of EMS revenues, computing contributed 21%, and communication accounted for 19%.

EMS gross margin declined 60 basis points sequentially to 8.3%, reflecting higher pass-through component costs and product-mix changes. However, operating margin improved to 3.3% from 2.4% in the prior quarter, supported by operating expense leverage.

Story Continues

Management noted that growing demand for AI accelerators contributed to computing revenue expansion, while elevated component costs continued to weigh on profitability.

ASE Technology Margins Expand

Consolidated gross profit increased 86.9% year over year to NT$53.97 billion. Gross margin expanded 500 basis points to 22.1%, reflecting stronger ATM revenues, favorable LEAP product mix and currency benefits.

Operating income surged 151% to NT$33.14 billion, while operating margin improved 580 basis points to 13.6%. Operating expenses increased to NT$20.82 billion, mainly due to higher headcount, profit-sharing expenses and research and development spending.

ATM gross margin reached 30.6%, up from 22.6% a year earlier, while operating margin expanded to 20% from 10.8%. Management indicated that increasing LEAP contributions have pushed profitability beyond the segment's previous structural margin ceiling.

ASX Investment Spending Moves Higher

Equipment capital expenditures totaled $2.10 billion during the third quarter, including $991 million for packaging operations, $1.07 billion for testing, $41 million for EMS and $5 million for interconnect materials and other activities.

The company additionally invested approximately $1.8 billion in facilities and land during the quarter. Management raised its 2026 capital expenditure budget to $11.5 billion from $10.5 billion, reflecting continued investment in semiconductor capacity expansion.

ASE Technology has 22 ongoing building projects in Taiwan, with more than half expected to begin supporting revenues by 2027. Management anticipates higher capital expenditures in 2027 as capacity constraints persist.

ASX Balance Sheet Remains Healthy

As of Sept. 30, 2026, ASE Technology held NT$107.94 billion in cash, cash equivalents and current financial assets. Total interest-bearing debt increased to NT$406.46 billion, while unused credit facilities totaled NT$457.28 billion. The net debt-to-equity ratio was 0.66.

Net cash generated from operating activities reached NT$50.46 billion during the quarter.

ASX Outlook Remains Strong

For the fourth quarter of 2026, management expects consolidated revenues to increase 6-8% sequentially in New Taiwan dollar terms. Gross margin is projected between 23% and 24%, while operating margin is expected in the 14.5-15.5% range. ATM revenues are forecast to grow 11-13% sequentially, with gross margin improving 100-200 basis points. EMS revenues are expected to remain relatively flat, with operating margin around 2%.

Management raised its 2026 LEAP revenue outlook to more than $4 billion and expects LEAP revenues to double in 2027. Full-process packaging revenues are projected to exceed $1 billion in 2027, while co-packaged optics revenues are expected to surpass $500 million, supported by sustained demand for advanced semiconductor technologies.

ASX Zacks Rank & Other Stocks to Consider

ASE Technology Holding currently flaunts a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy).

Some other top-ranked stocks in the broader Zacks Computer and Technology sector are Analog Devices ADI, Autodesk ADSK and Cisco Systems CSCO, each carrying a Zacks Rank #2 (Buy) at present. You can see the complete list of today's Zacks #1 Rank stocks here.

Shares of Analog Devices have rallied 85.3% year to date. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for ADI's fiscal 2026 earnings is pegged at $13.00 per share, up by 4 cents over the past 30 days, indicating an increase of 66.9% year over year.

Shares of Autodesk have plunged 19.6% year to date. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for ADSK's fiscal 2027 earnings is pegged at $12.62 per share, unchanged over the past 30 days, indicating a rise of 21% year over year.

Cisco Systems shares have surged 50.5% year to date. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for CSCO's fiscal 2027 earnings is pegged at $5.11 per share, unchanged over the past 30 days, indicating an increase of 18% year over year.

news.Title: What to Expect From Apple’s Q4
news.Content:
Apple (AAPL) will report its fourth-quarter earnings on Nov. 2. Strong demand for the iPhone and Mac is expected to support the company's performance, although supply constraints could limit sales growth.

AAPL stock has gained 28% so far this year and hit a new 52-week high of $351.73 on Oct. 23. The rally, supported by strong momentum in Apple's products and services businesses, has pushed the stock's valuation higher ahead of the Q4 earnings announcement. Let's take a closer look.

More News from Barchart

Elon Musk Invests $1 Billion in Skydance Stock. He Could Be Setting the Stage for a Major Starlink Deal.

'I Still Live A Great Life': Floyd Mayweather Says a Man 'Acting Like He Was A Friend' Stole $200 Million From Him

MRVL Stock Sinks as Marvell Technology Reportedly Considers Acquiring Lumentum

Tired of missing midday reversals? The FREE Barchart Brief newsletter keeps you in the know. Sign up now!

Supply Challenges Could Hurt Apple's Q4 Growth

Apple's Q4 report will likely reflect slower growth despite sustained demand for its core hardware products. During the Q3 earnings call, management indicated that customer demand for the iPhone and Mac remained robust but cautioned that supply constraints were expected to intensify sequentially, impacting growth.

Consequently, management projected total revenue growth of 9% to 11% year-over-year (YOY) for Q4. That signaled moderation from the stronger growth reported in the preceding quarter.

Apple delivered revenue of $109.4 billion in Q3, up 16% YOY. Performance remained broad-based, with every geographic segment recording double-digit growth. Product revenue increased 18% YOY to $78.7 billion, supported by strong contributions from the iPhone and Mac.

The iPhone remained Apple's largest revenue contributor, generating $54.3 billion, up 22% YOY. The iPhone 17 lineup drove growth, with double-digit gains across most markets. Apple also reported an all-time high in its active iPhone installed base and a June-quarter record for customers upgrading their devices. These indicators suggest that the company continues to benefit from customer retention, upgrade demand, and the strength of its broader ecosystem.

Mac revenue rose 29% YOY to $10.4 billion in Q3. The performance reflected strong demand for the MacBook Neo and MacBook Pro, with growth across both developed and emerging markets.

Although Apple expects iPhone demand to remain strong in the September quarter, management anticipates supply constraints and unfavorable foreign exchange movements will weigh on the reported growth rate. The company projected mid-teens YOY growth in iPhone revenue, below the 22% YOY growth achieved in Q3.

Story Continues

Apple's Services segment is expected to sustain momentum. Management indicated that Services revenue should grow at a pace broadly comparable to Q3. The segment generated $30.7 billion in Q3, an increase of 12% YOY.

The business benefits from Apple's extensive installed base of more than 2.5 billion active devices, which provides a substantial platform for recurring revenue generation. Paid subscriptions now exceed 1.5 billion, while both transacting accounts and paid accounts reached new quarterly records. The company also reported double-digit growth in these account categories across emerging markets. Advertising, the App Store, AppleCare, Apple Music, Apple TV+, cloud services, and payment-related offerings are among the businesses supporting this expansion.

The company's earnings outlook also suggests a more moderate growth trajectory in Q4. Slower revenue growth and higher memory costs could pressure margins and constrain earnings growth. Analysts expect Apple to report EPS of $1.98, representing about 7% YOY growth. This would mark a notable deceleration from the 29% increase in earnings reported in Q3. However, the previous quarter's comparison included a $0.11 per share benefit from tariff refunds.

Is Apple Stock a Buy?

Apple's Q4 performance is likely to be supported by resilient iPhone and Mac demand and continued Services growth, although supply constraints and higher memory costs could moderate revenue and earnings growth. With expected EPS growth slowing to 7% and AAPL stock trading near record highs, investors should take caution before going long on Apple shares ahead of earnings.

Overall, Wall Street analysts maintain a consensus "Moderate Buy" rating for Apple stock.

news.Title: VICR Gains From Hardware Boom and Rising Backlog: What's Ahead?
news.Content:
Vicor Corporation VICR is benefiting from rising demand for high-density power delivery solutions as AI processors, data centers, industrial platforms and defense applications require more efficient power conversion. Growth in Advanced Products, a rising backlog and expanding licensing income are supporting its revenue outlook. However, manufacturing capacity constraints, customer program timing and uneven royalty recognition remain key challenges.

Vicor's second-quarter 2026 revenues increased 1.6% year over year to $143.4 million, exceeding the consensus estimate by 3.13%. Excluding $45 million in patent litigation settlement revenues recorded in the year-ago quarter, revenues increased 49.3%. Advanced Products revenues surged 45% sequentially to $94.2 million, accounting for 65.7% of total revenues. Product revenues rose 31.8% year over year to $112.9 million, while royalty revenues increased to $30.4 million from $10.4 million.

Demand momentum remains strong across high-performance computing, industrial, aerospace and defense markets. Vicor's book-to-bill ratio remained above 1, while its 12-month backlog increased 145% year over year to approximately $379.7 million. Management expects third-quarter revenues to grow nearly 10% sequentially, supported by double-digit sequential growth in Advanced Products. Vicor is targeting more than $600 million in 2026 revenues, reflecting product growth and licensing income.

Vicor is expanding manufacturing capacity to support rising demand. Its first fabrication facility, Fab 1, is approaching full capacity utilization, with additional equipment being installed to increase output. The company is also evaluating sites for a second fabrication facility, which management considers necessary to achieve its long-term revenue objective of $2.5 billion.

Technology differentiation and intellectual property licensing provide additional growth opportunities. Vicor's Factorized Power Architecture and Vertical Power Delivery (VPD) technologies are designed to improve power efficiency and current density for increasingly demanding AI processors. Second-generation VPD development with its lead customer has reached an initial chipset baseline, while development systems are being introduced to additional original equipment manufacturers and hyperscalers.

How Competitors Fare Against VICR Stock

Vicor competes with Monolithic Power Systems MPWR and Analog Devices ADI. MPWR competes in high-performance power management for AI processors and data centers, while ADI competes in analog and power-management solutions for industrial, communications and computing applications.

Story Continues

Monolithic Power is benefiting from expanding power content across AI infrastructure, enterprise data and communications as customers adopt higher-density designs and module solutions. New customer ramps, platform refreshes and DDR5 orders expand its market, while sampling for 800-volt data-center architectures adds a growth avenue.

Analog Devices is benefiting from a broad-based recovery as Industrial demand improves and AI-related data center activity expands across optical and power applications. Long-cycle exposure to automation, test, aerospace and defense, energy systems and vehicle electrification supports durable growth.

VICR's Price Performance, Valuation and Estimates

Shares of Vicor have gained 88.5% year to date against the Zacks Electronics - Miscellaneous Components industry's decline of 20.2%.

The Zacks Consensus Estimate for VICR's 2026 and 2027 earnings implies year-over-year growth of 51% and 66%, respectively. The estimates for fiscal 2026 and 2027 have been revised upward in the past 30 days.
